prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate on which the committee is most broadly aligned: three first-place rankings and six top-three placements, with only two members placing it below sixth. The science is an unusually clean pairing of an original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift while keeping many atoms in a Lamb-Dicke regime) with a decisive experimental follow-through (Ye's group taking strontium clocks to the 1e-18 regime and demonstrating many-body-controlled operation). The consequences are measurable rather than promised: international clock comparisons over fibre, millimetre-scale relativistic redshift, constraints on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and the roadmap to a redefined SI second. From my own experimental background I value that this is a result whose systematic uncertainty budgets have been reproduced by several independent laboratories, so the claim does not rest on one team's analysis. Two names give a defensible and uncontroversial three-person limit, with room to spare.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control, optical ion clocks) cover the surrounding toolbox, and Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits partly inside the 2005 territory, so the committee must be able to state what is genuinely new in the lattice clock. I believe it can (the neutral-atom magic-wavelength scheme, with its stability advantage from large atom numbers), but the citation has to be written narrowly. A second concern is that other pioneers (for example Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto) are outside the two credited names and I am relying on memory for the fine priority history. Finally, the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue for waiting; I do not find that persuasive, since the science stands independent of the metrological convention.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery (B057) first, arguing the 2013 prize recognised only the theory, the measurement is a discovery in the plainest sense and it is fully mature and arguably overdue, while accepting that credit rests on founding leaders and not on discovery-day analyses.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on maturity: B057 is the strongest case in scientific significance, and I rank it as my first alternative. Where I disagree is on whether it is ready for this prize. I have worked in large collaborations and know that the three credited names are the founding project leaders of ATLAS and CMS, which rewards instrument creation and not the 2012 observation itself, and the analyses that produced the signal belong to many people outside the trio. Unlike lattice clocks, where invention and demonstration sit with two identifiable groups, the Higgs measurement cannot be assigned cleanly without a policy decision on collaboration credit. If the committee is prepared to take that decision, I would not resist B057; I would not make it the lead on the present attribution.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B042 first as a simple, original idea with a coherence-control and laser-spectroscopy basis, giving 1e-18-class performance confirmed by independent labs for more than a decade, and calls it arguably overdue, while noting that Hall and Haensch combs (2005) are outside the supplied credit.
responses.response: I share Kroll's reading of the maturity and the clean two-name allocation, and I value his hands-on knowledge of the spectroscopy, which I lack. I would qualify one point: 'overdue' should not be taken to mean the 2005 prize is irrelevant. The citation must say that the contribution is the lattice trapping at the magic wavelength and the resulting accuracy and stability, so that nobody can read the prize as a second award for combs. I also ask Kroll to say whether, in his judgement, the stability advantage from interrogating many atoms simultaneously is the point that truly separates this from the ion clocks recognised in 2012, because that is the argument I would put forward against the novelty objection.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B033 (dynamical mean-field theory) first and puts B042 sixth, citing overlap with the earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes, the not-yet-completed SI redefinition and blurred attribution among clock groups, though he acknowledges strong confirmation at the 1e-18 level.
responses.response: Eriksson's novelty objection is the serious one against B042 and I do not dismiss it, but I think it conflates the enabling toolbox with the invention. Combs gave access to optical frequencies and ion clocks demonstrated single-system control, whereas the lattice clock's contribution is a distinct way of reaching a new regime of stability and systematic control, which neither prior prize covers. On the pending redefinition I disagree that timing is early: the prize rewards the demonstration, not a decision by the CGPM. Regarding his own B033, I accept that DMFT is a very mature framework, but he himself flags that Metzner is not among the credited names and that DFT+DMFT is partly contested in its first-principles claims, which makes both the attribution and the discovery-versus-method status less clean than for the clocks.

responses.point: Johansson ranks trapped-ion and cold-atom quantum computing foundations (B038) first, citing the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal and its experimental realisation as the intellectual base of hardware quantum computing, while recognising overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize and that Blatt's role differs from Wineland's and Monroe's.
responses.response: I accept that the Cirac-Zoller proposal is a landmark and that it is mature. My reservation is about what the prize would honour: the 2012 prize already recognised the control of individual trapped quantum systems, and the candidate bundles gate theory, ion experiments and cold-atom simulation, so a prize that omits Wineland and Monroe would be hard to defend historically. Johansson's own point on this overlap is, I think, stronger against B038 than the comb and ion-clock overlap is against B042, because the lattice-clock scheme is separable from earlier work and the attribution is two clean names. I place B038 below my alternatives for this reason, although I would value hearing from him how he would narrow the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to restrict the citation narrowly to the lattice-clock scheme in view of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work is considered separable.

Whether other lattice-clock pioneers outside the credited names (for example Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto) have claims that would make a two-person prize contested; I rely on memory for the priority history.
Whether the committee is ready to adopt a convention for crediting large-collaboration discoveries, which would change the ranking of B057 relative to B042.
Whether the pending SI redefinition should delay recognition, a view I do not hold but cannot exclude among colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B042: my documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH) do not involve the optical lattice clock community. For my alternative B057 I note that I have experience of large detector collaborations and of accelerator-based experimental physics from my doctoral background, which gives familiarity but no recorded tie to ATLAS or CMS or to the credited names. I will recuse myself from any candidate where a connection emerges.
